subChunks.title: Genetic Genealogy as a Business

storyBeats.txt: Genetic genealogy has moved from hobbyist enthusiasm to professional specialism faster than almost any other area of our discipline, Theodora said. Clients are arriving with DNA tests and no idea what to do with them. Law enforcement is contracting genealogists for investigative work. Heir hunters are using DNA where paper trails have failed.

The business of genetic genealogy is different from the business of conventional genealogical research. The technical complexity is higher, the ethical constraints are sharper, and the potential for both great help and serious harm is amplified.

Building a sustainable practice in this area requires not only technical mastery of DNA analysis — which you have developed across this pathway — but also the ability to scope projects appropriately, communicate results clearly, and navigate sensitive discoveries without causing harm.

subChunks.hookHtml:
Genetic genealogy services have become one of the fastest-growing areas of professional genealogical practice. Clients range from individuals overwhelmed by their DNA match lists to law enforcement agencies seeking to identify cold-case suspects. Services range from simple match-list interpretation to full investigative genetic genealogy projects requiring months of tree-building work.

Building a viable professional practice in genetic genealogy requires combining technical DNA competency with the same project management, client communication, and ethical practice skills required in conventional genealogical work — plus an additional layer of specialised ethics and legal awareness specific to genetic data.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Service Offerings in Genetic Genealogy

Professional genetic genealogy services fall into several categories:

  • DNA interpretation: Reviewing a client's existing test results, explaining what they show, and identifying the most promising matches for further research. The entry-level service; often offered as a one-off consultation rather than an ongoing project.
  • Unknown parentage research: Full research project using DNA combined with documentary research to identify a biological parent or family. Typically the most intensive service; multiple platforms, Leeds Method clustering, mirror trees, documentary corroboration.
  • Ethnic heritage research: Interpreting ethnicity estimates, researching the family origins suggested by DNA, and contextualising results within historical migration patterns.
  • DNA health interpretation: NOT a genealogical service — health genetic counselling requires clinical credentials and falls outside genealogical professional scope. Genealogists who receive health-related DNA questions should refer clients to genetic counsellors.
  • Investigative genetic genealogy (IGG): Law enforcement or heir-location DNA work. Requires specific ethical protocols, typically delivered under contract with institutional clients rather than directly to the public.

Pricing Genetic Genealogy Services

Pricing models for genetic genealogy services: (1) hourly billing (the most common for research work — uncertain scope requires flexibility); (2) fixed-fee packages for defined deliverables (e.g., 'DNA match list interpretation report — 2 hours of analysis and written summary'); (3) retainer arrangements for law enforcement or heir-location clients requiring ongoing availability.

Market rates vary significantly by geography, credential level, and service type. Professional genealogists with recognised credentials (BCG CG, ICAPGen AG) and demonstrable DNA specialisms command higher rates. Rates for investigative genetic genealogy work by qualified specialists can significantly exceed conventional genealogical research rates.

Scoping DNA Projects

DNA projects are notoriously difficult to scope in advance. A client with a complex unknown parentage case and no close matches may require 40+ hours of tree-building work; a client with a first cousin as their highest match may be resolved in 4 hours. This scope uncertainty must be communicated clearly in the research plan.

Best practice: agree a set number of research hours (e.g., 10 hours initial project); provide a milestone report at the midpoint; and offer the client a go/no-go decision before committing further resources. This protects both client and researcher from unexpectedly large projects.

Client Communication in DNA Projects

DNA project clients often have a high emotional investment in the results. Unknown parentage clients may be searching for a sense of identity. This requires communication that is: technically accurate (not falsely optimistic); emotionally sensitive (sensitive to the distress that unexpected findings may cause); and professionally boundaried (the genealogist's role is to provide information, not emotional support — refer to appropriate counsellors when needed).

Managing expectations before testing: ensure clients understand that DNA testing may reveal unexpected findings — NPEs, unknown half-siblings, donor conception. This conversation is easier before testing than after. Document it in the client intake process.

Legal and Regulatory Considerations

Genetic genealogy businesses must comply with: data protection legislation (GDPR for UK/EU clients; applicable US state laws); consumer protection legislation; and any specific DNA-testing regulations in the relevant jurisdiction. In the UK, the Human Tissue Act 2004 governs the use of biological samples and imposes licensing requirements on businesses that process DNA. Consumer-facing genealogical DNA services require compliance with the Act.

Professional indemnity insurance is strongly advisable for professional genealogists and essential for those handling sensitive genetic data. Specialist professional liability policies covering genealogical practice are available through organisations including APG.

Building a Genetic Genealogy Business

Practical steps: define your service offerings clearly (what you will and won't do); set your rates and billing model; establish client intake procedures (intake form, engagement letter, terms of service); build a referral network (other genealogists, genetic counsellors, ancestry DNA community groups); maintain continuing education in the rapidly evolving DNA field; and develop a professional online presence that communicates your specialism and credentials.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what a professional genetic genealogist does — what services they offer, who their clients are, and why it's a distinct professional specialism rather than just something anyone with a DNA test can do.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A new client contacts you for help with her DNA results. She says: 'I did a test on AncestryDNA and I have hundreds of matches and I don't understand any of it. I just want to know where my ancestors came from — specifically whether the family tradition that we have Native American ancestry is true.' Write the initial response you would send to this client, covering: what services you could offer, what the cost might be, and what you would need from her to proceed.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Dear [Client],

Thank you for getting in touch. DNA results can be overwhelming at first, but the questions you're asking are very answerable with the right approach.

I offer a DNA interpretation service that would address both of your questions directly. Here's what I'd propose:

Initial consultation (1 hour, £[rate]): We review your AncestryDNA results together, I explain what your matches and ethnicity estimate actually show, and we identify whether any matches might connect to your family's tradition of Native American heritage. This would give you a clear picture of what the DNA shows and a realistic assessment of the specific claim.

Follow-up research (if needed, quoted per project): If the initial review suggests there may be a genuine Native American connection worth investigating, I can research the specific family lines indicated by your matches, using both DNA clustering and documentary records, and prepare a written report of findings. This type of project typically takes 4–8 hours depending on match complexity.

Before we proceed, I should mention one important point about DNA and Native American ancestry claims specifically: AncestryDNA's ethnicity estimates for Indigenous American populations have significant limitations, and a claim of Native American heritage is not conclusively verifiable from an ethnicity estimate alone. I can help you understand exactly what your results do and don't show.

To get started, I'd ask you to: (1) share your AncestryDNA login details securely (or download and share your match list); (2) complete our client intake form covering your known family background; and (3) confirm your approval of the initial consultation fee.

I look forward to helping you explore your heritage.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Design the terms of service / engagement letter for a genetic genealogy practice. Include: (1) scope of services (what you will and won't do); (2) billing terms; (3) what happens if unexpected findings are made; (4) data protection and confidentiality obligations; (5) a clause about referring clients to other professionals when needed. Keep it professional but accessible to a non-specialist client.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Engagement Terms for [Practice Name] Genetic Genealogy Services

1. Services
[Practice Name] provides genetic genealogy research services including DNA result interpretation, unknown parentage research, and ethnic heritage research. We do not provide medical, legal, or psychological advice. We do not offer health-related genetic interpretation — clients with questions about health-related DNA results should consult a qualified genetic counsellor. We do not conduct investigative genetic genealogy for law enforcement without a separately negotiated institutional contract.

2. Fees and billing
Research services are billed at [£X] per hour. Fees are charged for researcher time and expertise regardless of research outcome — genealogical research cannot guarantee specific findings. A written estimate of likely hours will be provided before work begins. Work will not proceed beyond agreed milestones without client approval. Invoices are payable within 14 days. A signed copy of this agreement is required before work commences.

3. Unexpected findings
Genetic genealogy research may reveal information that was not anticipated and may be significant or distressing — including non-paternity events, previously unknown biological relatives, or health-related information visible in genealogical DNA data. We will disclose all findings to the commissioning client only. We recommend that clients consider these possibilities before commissioning research. If findings require specialist support, we will provide referrals to appropriate counselling or advisory services.

4. Data protection and confidentiality
All client information, including DNA data, family history information, and research findings, will be held in confidence and not shared with any third party without written client consent, except as required by law. Data will be stored securely in accordance with applicable data protection legislation (UK GDPR). Clients may request deletion of their data at any time. We will not use client DNA data for any purpose other than the commissioned research.

5. Professional referrals
Where research requires expertise beyond our specialism, or where a client's needs extend into medical, legal, or psychological territory, we will advise accordingly and provide referrals to appropriate professionals. Our duty is to the client's best interests, including recognising the limits of our own professional scope.
learningObjectives: Identify the service categories within professional genetic genealogy practice and their distinct client bases.
Design a scoping and milestone structure for DNA research projects that manages uncertain scope appropriately.
Describe the data protection and regulatory obligations specific to a UK-based genetic genealogy business.
Draft client-facing documentation (engagement letter, terms of service) appropriate for genetic genealogy practice.
commonMistakes: Offering to interpret health-related DNA results without clinical genetics training — this falls outside genealogical scope and creates legal liability.
Accepting a DNA project without documenting scope, fees, and unexpected-findings provisions in writing beforehand.
Failing to manage client expectations about Native American or other population-specific ethnicity estimate limitations.
Not carrying professional indemnity insurance when handling sensitive genetic data.
assessmentCriteria: Service offerings are clearly defined and appropriately exclude out-of-scope activities (health interpretation, law enforcement work without institutional contract).
Billing and scoping provisions address the inherent uncertainty of DNA research project scope.
Data protection and confidentiality obligations meet GDPR requirements.
Unexpected-findings clause prepares clients appropriately without being alarmist.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: UK legislation governing the use and storage of biological samples including DNA; businesses processing DNA for analytical purposes require compliance with its licensing provisions.
Insurance covering professional liability for errors, omissions, or negligence in professional services; essential for genealogists handling sensitive DNA data.
A healthcare professional specialising in genetic risk assessment and counselling; the appropriate referral for clients with health-related questions arising from genealogical DNA testing.

A written agreement between researcher and client specifying services, fees, scope, confidentiality, and other terms before work commences — the essential contractual foundation of professional practice.

questions.questionHtml: A client asks you to interpret the health risk information shown in their 23andMe results. How should you respond?
options: Provide the interpretation — DNA is DNA whether it's genealogical or health-related
Decline and refer them to a qualified genetic counsellor — health genetic interpretation falls outside genealogical professional scope and requires clinical credentials
Provide a brief informal assessment but emphasise it is not medical advice
Charge a higher rate and proceed, ensuring the client signs a disclaimer
questions.correctAnswer: Decline and refer them to a qualified genetic counsellor — health genetic interpretation falls outside genealogical professional scope and requires clinical credentials
questions.explanationHtml: Health genetic interpretation requires clinical genetics training and is regulated as a medical activity in most jurisdictions. A genealogist who provides health genetic advice outside their competence and scope risks both professional liability and client harm. The appropriate response is to decline and provide a referral to a certified genetic counsellor.

questions.questionHtml: A client's DNA unknown parentage project is proving more complex than anticipated — you have now spent 15 hours on a project you estimated at 5 hours and have not yet identified the biological parent. What should you do?
options: Continue until the project is complete without informing the client of the additional hours
Stop work at the agreed milestone, provide a progress report documenting what has been done, ruled out, and identified, and discuss with the client whether to continue, adjust scope, or conclude
Refund the client's fees since you did not deliver the expected result
Renegotiate the hourly rate downward to compensate for the underestimate
questions.correctAnswer: Stop work at the agreed milestone, provide a progress report documenting what has been done, ruled out, and identified, and discuss with the client whether to continue, adjust scope, or conclude
questions.explanationHtml: Professional practice requires transparency about scope and cost. The milestone system exists precisely to prevent this situation — the client should have been informed at the 5-hour milestone that the project was more complex than anticipated. At that point, the client can make an informed decision about whether to invest further resources. Continuing without informing the client of additional hours is a breach of professional obligations.

questions.questionHtml: Why do professional genetic genealogists typically charge for time rather than for results?
options: Because results-based billing would incentivise genealogists to fabricate findings

Because genealogical research outcomes are inherently uncertain — the researcher can guarantee their time, expertise, and methodology, but not that the specific ancestral connection or biological family will be identified
Because time-based billing is required by APG ethics
Because DNA analysis results are always inconclusive
questions.correctAnswer: Because genealogical research outcomes are inherently uncertain — the researcher can guarantee their time, expertise, and methodology, but not that the specific ancestral connection or biological family will be identified
questions.explanationHtml: The fundamental uncertainty of genealogical research means that billing for results is not workable — a researcher may spend 40 hours and not identify a biological parent through no fault of their own, simply because the relevant family members have not tested. Fee-for-time is the professional model because it accurately reflects what the researcher can guarantee: their expertise and effort, not a specific finding.
